away.about: Life... Finds a Way is a reaction image of Dr. Ian Malcolm, played by Jeff Goldblum in Jurassic Park, delivering his famous warning about nature's unpredictability. It is used to caption situations where something happens despite every attempt to prevent it, or where a workaround appears against all odds.
away.origin: The line comes from the 1993 film Jurassic Park, where Malcolm argues that the park's dinosaurs will inevitably breed.

badchoice.about: Milk Was a Bad Choice shows Ron Burgundy (Will Ferrell) regretfully drinking a carton of milk on a hot day in Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy. The meme captions any decision that seemed fine at the time but turns out to be an obviously poor idea.
badchoice.origin: In the 2004 comedy Anchorman, Ron wanders San Diego after losing his job and mutters "Milk was a bad choice" while sweating in the sun.

because.about: This Men in Black template shows Agent J (Will Smith) in the scene where he talks about being judged for driving a nice car, then admits he stole it, but not for the reason assumed. It is used for two-part jokes that set up an assumption and then undercut it with a twist.
because.origin: The scene is from the 1997 film Men in Black, during the recruitment test sequence.

aka: Brad Pitt What's in the Box
box.about: What's in the Box!? is a reaction image of Detective Mills (Brad Pitt) screaming in the climax of the thriller Se7en. It is used to express desperate curiosity or dread about an unopened package, an unread message, or any unknown contents.
box.origin: The scene is the ending of David Fincher's 1995 film Se7en, in which a box is delivered to the detectives in the desert.

bs.about: This is Bull, Shark is a pun-based reaction image of a shark used to call something nonsense in a lighthearted way, playing on the bull shark species name. It typically pairs a sarcastic setup with a punchline about being fooled or caught out.
bs.origin: The image spread on Reddit's r/funny in 2015 as a caption pun about bull sharks.

buzz.about: X, X Everywhere is a two-panel image of Woody and Buzz Lightyear from Toy Story, with Buzz gesturing at the horizon. The caption follows the template "X. X everywhere" to complain that something has become ubiquitous, from memes to bugs in code.
buzz.origin: The still comes from the 1995 Pixar film Toy Story and became an image macro in the early 2010s.

aka: I Was Told There Would Be Cake
cake.about: Office Space Milton is an image of the mumbling office worker Milton Waddams from the film Office Space, often captioned with the line "I was told there would be cake." It expresses disappointment when a promised reward, perk, or event never materializes.
cake.origin: Milton, played by Stephen Root, is a character in the 1999 comedy Office Space; the cake line references the birthday scene where he is left without a slice.

aka: Look at Me I'm the Captain Now
captain.about: I Am the Captain Now is a reaction image of the pirate Muse (Barkhad Abdi) from Captain Phillips declaring "Look at me. I'm the captain now." It is used whenever someone, or something, takes control of a situation, a device, or a conversation.
captain.origin: The line is from the 2013 film Captain Phillips, in which Somali pirates board a cargo ship.

cbg.about: Comic Book Guy is the sarcastic, overweight owner of the Android's Dungeon comic shop in The Simpsons, famous for the catchphrase "Worst. Episode. Ever." The meme is used to deliver an exaggerated, snobbish verdict on anything, usually in the "Worst. X. Ever." format.
cbg.origin: Comic Book Guy first appeared in The Simpsons in 1991, and the "Worst episode ever" line became a fan catchphrase in the late 1990s.

country.about: What a Country! is a reaction image of Dr. Nick Riviera from The Simpsons, delighted at a surprising fact, usually captioned "Inflammable means flammable? What a country!" It is used to react with mock amazement to an absurd rule, contradiction, or discovery.
country.origin: The line is spoken by Dr. Nick in The Simpsons episode "Trilogy of Error" (2001).

fine.about: This is Fine shows a cartoon dog sitting calmly with a cup of coffee while the room around him burns, saying "This is fine." It is one of the most widely used memes for denial, forced calm, or pretending everything is under control while a situation collapses.
fine.origin: The panels come from KC Green's 2013 webcomic Gunshow, strip #648 "On Fire".

firsttry.about: First Try! is a celebratory reaction image used when something works on the very first attempt, sarcastically or not. It is a popular caption for coding, gaming, and DIY moments where beginner's luck strikes.
firsttry.origin: The template spread through gaming clips and reaction videos celebrating a lucky first attempt.

genie.about: Genie Lamp is a two-panel template from Disney's Aladdin in which the Genie boasts "Phenomenal cosmic power!" and then deflates with "Itty bitty living space." It contrasts something grand or powerful with a cramped, disappointing reality.
genie.origin: The exchange is from the 1992 animated film Aladdin, voiced by Robin Williams.

grumpycat.about: Grumpy Cat is the famously frowning cat Tardar Sauce, whose permanently annoyed expression became one of the internet's most recognizable memes. Captions express pessimism, refusal, and deadpan disapproval, often ending in a flat "NO."
grumpycat.origin: Photos of Tardar Sauce were posted to Reddit in September 2012 and went viral within days.

aka: I Should Not Have Said That
hagrid.about: I Should Not Have Said That is a reaction image of Hagrid from Harry Potter looking regretful after letting slip a secret. It is used when someone realizes they have said too much or revealed something they were supposed to keep quiet.
hagrid.origin: The line is from Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (2001), when Hagrid accidentally mentions Nicolas Flamel.

handshake.about: Epic Handshake is an object-labeling template of two muscular arms clasping hands, taken from the film Predator. Each arm is labeled with a different group or idea and the handshake represents the one thing they unexpectedly agree on.
handshake.origin: The handshake between Dutch (Arnold Schwarzenegger) and Dillon (Carl Weathers) is from the 1987 film Predator and became a labeling meme in the late 2010s.

ive.about: Jony Ive Redesigns Things features Apple's former chief design officer against a white background, parodying the earnest tone of Apple product videos. Captions mock minimalist redesigns that remove useful features while insisting "we think you'll love it."
ive.origin: The meme parodies Apple's product introduction videos narrated by Jony Ive in the early 2010s.

joker.about: It's Simple, Kill the Batman shows Heath Ledger's Joker from The Dark Knight calmly proposing his plan to Gotham's mob bosses. The meme is used to present an outrageously blunt solution to a complicated problem as if it were obvious.
joker.origin: The line is from the 2008 film The Dark Knight, during the Joker's meeting with the mob.

jw.about: Probably Not a Good Idea is a reaction image of Owen Grady (Chris Pratt) in Jurassic World reacting to the news that the park created a new hybrid dinosaur. It captions any plan that is clearly going to end badly.
jw.origin: The scene is from the 2015 film Jurassic World.

kombucha.about: Kombucha Girl is a two-panel reaction image of Brittany Tomlinson tasting kombucha, first grimacing and then reconsidering with a thoughtful nod. It captures the feeling of initially hating something and then warming up to it.
kombucha.origin: The clip came from a TikTok video posted in August 2019 that went viral across Twitter and Instagram.

light.about: Everything the Light Touches is Our Kingdom is a template from The Lion King in which Mufasa shows Simba their kingdom and warns him about the shadowy place beyond their borders. It is used to label a wholesome domain versus a forbidden or dreaded area.
light.origin: The scene is from Disney's 1994 animated film The Lion King.

michael-scott.about: Michael Scott No God No is a reaction image of Michael Scott from The Office screaming "No, God! No, God, please, no!" in dread. It is used to react to terrible news or the return of something you hoped was gone for good.
michael-scott.origin: The scene is from The Office (US) season 5 episode "Prince Family Paper", when Toby returns to the office.

nails.about: Guy Hammering Nails Into Sand is a photo of a man kneeling on a beach, hammering nails into the sand, used for pointless or futile effort. Labels are placed on the hammer, the nails, and the sand to describe an activity that accomplishes nothing.
nails.origin: The photo circulated in 2019 as a "when the boss is coming and you need to look busy" joke before becoming a labeling template.

noah.about: What the Hell is This? is a multi-panel Family Guy template in which Noah loads animals onto the ark, accepts two familiar ones, and then recoils at a strange third creature. It is used to mock an awkward hybrid or a category that does not fit anywhere.
noah.origin: The panels come from a Family Guy cutaway gag about Noah's Ark; the "street / road / stroad" caption popularized the format.

prop3.about: Too Confusing, Too Extreme is a parody of a 2022 Michigan political ad slogan, applied to anything mildly complicated to make it sound dangerous. It is used to mock fear-mongering over ordinary things like zipper merging or daylight saving time.
prop3.origin: The phrase comes from campaign ads opposing Michigan's Proposal 3 in the 2022 election, which were widely parodied online.

aka: Oh, Is That What We're Going to Do Today?
red.about: Oh, Is That What We're Going to Do Today? is a reaction image of Red Forman from That '70s Show squaring up with a sarcastic "We're going to fight?" It is used to respond to a challenge or provocation with unimpressed confidence.
red.origin: Red Forman, played by Kurtwood Smith, is the grumpy father in That '70s Show (1998-2006).

regret.about: I Immediately Regret This Decision is a reaction image of Ron Burgundy (Will Ferrell) from Anchorman, shouted after he jumps into a bear enclosure. It captions any choice that goes wrong the instant it is made.
regret.origin: The line is from the 2004 comedy Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy.

right.about: Anakin and Padme Change the World For the Better is a four-panel template from Star Wars: Attack of the Clones. Anakin makes a statement, Padme smiles and asks a clarifying question ("for the better, right?"), Anakin stays silent, and Padme repeats the question with growing worry.
right.origin: The stills are from the picnic scene in Star Wars: Episode II (2002); the format went viral in May 2021.

sad-boehner.about: Sad John Boehner is a reaction image of the former Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives looking sorrowful, referencing his well-known tendency to cry in public. It is used as a lighthearted "sad politician" template, often captioned with reasons for disappointment.
sad-boehner.origin: John Boehner served as Speaker from 2011 to 2015 and was frequently photographed tearing up during speeches.

sad-clinton.about: Sad Bill Clinton is a reaction image of the former U.S. president looking dejected, used to express disappointment or feeling let down. It belongs to a family of "sad politician" templates paired with captions about what caused the sadness.
sad-clinton.origin: The photo of Bill Clinton, president from 1993 to 2001, circulated as a reaction image in the mid 2010s.

sf.about: Sealed Fate is an advice-animal style image of a wide-eyed seal that appears to be bracing for disaster. Captions describe the moment right before an inevitable consequence, like realizing your parents heard you swear.
sf.origin: The seal photo spread on Reddit's r/AdviceAnimals in 2015 as the "impending doom seal."

snek.about: Skeptical Snake is a reaction image of a snake with a narrowed, doubtful expression, used to express suspicion or disbelief. Captions typically describe a situation that looks normal but is not quite right.
snek.origin: The photo spread on Reddit in December 2016 under the title "Skeptical snake."

sohappy.about: I Would Be So Happy is a reaction template built around a hopeful wish and the joy it would bring, following the format "if X, I would be so happy." It is used both sincerely and sarcastically to express longing for a simple outcome.
sohappy.origin: The line and image spread from a video clip in which the speaker describes a small thing that would make them extremely happy.

sohot.about: So Hot Right Now is a reaction image of fashion mogul Mugatu from Zoolander exclaiming "Hansel. So hot right now." It is used to point out whatever is currently trendy or popular, often with a hint of sarcasm.
sohot.origin: The line is from the 2001 comedy Zoolander, spoken by Will Ferrell's character Mugatu.

sparta.about: This is Sparta! shows King Leonidas from the film 300 mid-shout as he kicks a Persian messenger into a pit. The meme, and its "This. Is. X!" caption format, is used for over-the-top, dramatic declarations.
sparta.origin: The scene is from the 2006 film 300, and the line became one of the earliest viral movie quote memes.

aka: Baby, You've Got a Stew Going
stew.about: Baby, You've Got a Stew Going is a reaction image of Carl Weathers from Arrested Development proudly delivering his thrifty cooking advice. It is used to celebrate making something worthwhile out of leftovers, scraps, or a modest situation.
stew.origin: The line is from Arrested Development season 1 (2004), where Carl Weathers plays a frugal version of himself.

waygd.about: What Are Ya Gonna Do? is a resigned-shrug reaction image used to accept an unfortunate situation that cannot be changed. The caption sets up the problem and the punchline shrugs it off.
waygd.origin: The template comes from a video clip of a man shrugging and asking "what are ya gonna do?" that spread as a reaction GIF.

wishes.about: Genie Rules is a template in which the Genie from Aladdin lays out the rules of wishing, and the caption adds a fourth, absurd rule or a wish so ridiculous the Genie refuses it. It is used to joke about impossible requests, like dividing by zero.
wishes.origin: The image is from Disney's 1992 film Aladdin, where the Genie explains his three rules; the format spread in 2019.

cryingfloor.about: Crying on Floor is a two-panel template in which a friend tries to comfort someone who has collapsed on the floor in tears. The top caption is the reassurance and the bottom caption is the absurdly minor thing that caused the breakdown.
cryingfloor.origin: The image spread on Know Your Meme and Reddit in 2016 alongside the Game of Thrones "Hold the Door" episode reactions.

aka: What Color Do You Want Your Dragon
dragon.about: What Color Do You Want Your Dragon is a comic-style template from Tumblr in which someone is granted a wish, answers with something ordinary, and is met with the exasperated reply about what color they want their dragon. It is used for wishes and requests that get spectacularly misheard or ignored.
dragon.origin: The comic circulated on Tumblr and was catalogued on Know Your Meme in 2016.

millers.about: You Guys Are Getting Paid? is a four-panel template from the comedy We're the Millers in which each character discovers the others are being paid far more, ending with Kenny's shocked "You guys are getting paid?" It is used to rank how badly different groups are treated in the same situation.
millers.origin: The stills come from the 2013 film We're the Millers; the format took off as a meme in 2020.

ptj.about: Phoebe Teaching Joey is an eight-panel template from Friends in which Phoebe patiently says a phrase piece by piece, Joey repeats each piece correctly, and then says something completely different when he puts it together. It is used to mock someone who follows every step and still reaches the wrong conclusion.
ptj.origin: The scene is from the Friends episode "The One Where Joey Speaks French" (season 10, 2004).

aka: Zoolander Sees Hansel on the Red Carpet
zoolander.about: Zoolander Walk-Off Stare is a split-screen of Derek Zoolander (Ben Stiller) and Hansel (Owen Wilson) locking eyes across the red carpet in the 2001 comedy Zoolander. The format took off on TikTok in late 2022 alongside the "lightskin stare" trend: a caption describes an awkward, cringey, or oddly relatable moment while the two models stare each other down.
zoolander.origin: The frame comes from the red-carpet scene in Zoolander (2001) that leads to the walk-off; the meme spread in November and December 2022, usually set to "Who Is She?" by I Monster.

kittens.about: Three Kittens Dancing is the AI-generated TikTok video of three fluffy kittens standing upright and dancing in perfect sync, often captioned as "the dark triad" or used as a green-screen template. The trio's deadpan choreography makes it a go-to format for any group of three, from friends to symptoms to your three unfinished tasks.
kittens.origin: TikTok user @meowtakeover posted the original Sora-generated clip on June 28th, 2026, set to "Spencer Hill Cool" by GFY1994; within weeks it had tens of millions of views and countless edits, remixes and dance recreations.

leo-cheers.about: Leonardo DiCaprio Cheers is a still of Jay Gatsby raising a champagne glass toward the camera with a knowing smile, from the 2013 film The Great Gatsby. It is used to toast, congratulate, or sarcastically salute whoever the caption describes.
leo-cheers.origin: The frame comes from the party scene in Baz Luhrmann's The Great Gatsby (2013) and became a reaction image the same year.

theydontknow.about: They Don't Know shows a Wojak in a party hat standing alone in the corner of a party, thinking a caption that starts with "They don't know…". It is used for private thoughts, niche obsessions, or secrets that nobody around you would care about.
theydontknow.origin: The drawing spread on 4chan and Reddit in early 2020 and became a caption template for awkward, self-aware thoughts.

cardboard.about: Guy Holding Cardboard Sign is a photo of a man in a crowd holding a blank cardboard sign above his head, ready for whatever message the caption writes on it. It is a general-purpose format for unpopular opinions, announcements, and public service reminders.
cardboard.origin: The blank-sign photo circulated as an exploitable in 2019 and stays popular because the sign fits any short statement.

homelander.about: Homelander Stare is a still of Homelander from The Boys (Antony Starr) glaring over a phone with a tight, barely contained expression. It captions moments of silent rage, disbelief, or the calm before an overreaction.
homelander.origin: The shot is from Amazon's The Boys, and the stare became a reaction image during the show's fourth season in 2024.

homer-bush.about: Homer Backs Into the Bushes is the reaction GIF of Homer Simpson slowly stepping backward into a hedge until he vanishes. It is the universal way to say "I'm going to pretend I was never here" after an embarrassing moment.
homer-bush.origin: The clip is from The Simpsons season 5 episode "Homer Loves Flanders" (1994) and became one of the internet's most reused GIFs.

coffin.about: Coffin Dance shows the Ghanaian dancing pallbearers carrying a casket in step, forever paired with the song "Astronomia" by Vicetone and Tony Igy. The meme caps off any clip or caption where someone is about to meet their doom, from a bad decision to a Friday deploy.
coffin.origin: The pallbearers, led by Benjamin Aidoo, were filmed by BBC in 2017; the clips took over TikTok and YouTube in early 2020 as the go-to punchline for fatal mistakes.

aka: Japanese Parliament Trying to Stop Shinichi Yokoyama
would.about: Would (Japanese Parliament) is the photo of a dozen Japanese lawmakers physically restraining committee chairman Shinichi Yokoyama as he shouts into a microphone. Captioned with a single "would", it became the definitive image for blurting out an opinion everyone around you is trying to stop, and the flagship of the "would" reaction-image family.
would.origin: The photo was taken on December 8th, 2018, during a chaotic vote on Japan's immigration reform bill; it resurfaced as a reaction image in 2022 and was crowned the canonical "would" picture on Reddit and Twitter.

wood.about: Would (Literally Wood) is the pun version of the "would" reaction image: a photo of actual wood captioned "would". It gets posted in reply to attractive people, food, or anything else worth a "would", and the joke is that it is, literally, wood.
wood.origin: "Would" reaction images (animals and people at a microphone saying "would") took off in late 2022; the wood puns followed on Reddit and Twitter, with lumber, logs, and hardware-store products captioned "would". Photo: Jared from Harrisburg, PA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

verity.about: Verity Live Reaction is a still of a yellow Minecraft-style face with a worried expression, used as a "live reaction" caption for watching something go wrong in real time. It took off in 2026 as a cleaner, cuter alternative to the classic Live Tucker Reaction format.
verity.origin: The image spread on TikTok and imgflip in mid-2026 as a reaction template for edits and commentary videos.

lanterns.about: Lanterns Interrogation is a three-panel template from HBO's Lanterns (2026) in which Kyle Chandler's Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre's John Stewart question a suspect. The panels set up a question, a stare, and a verdict, which makes it a natural format for grilling someone about a bad decision.
lanterns.origin: The stills come from the interrogation scene in Lanterns, the Green Lantern series released in 2026, and spread on imgflip within weeks of the episode.

aka: Moe Throws Barney Out of the Bar
moe-barney.about: Moe Throws Barney is a three-panel Simpsons template in which Moe grabs Barney, hauls him to the door, and throws him out of the tavern. Each panel gets a label, so it's the go-to format for anything being unceremoniously kicked out of somewhere.
moe-barney.origin: The scene is from The Simpsons; the three-panel version has been an object-labeling template on Reddit since 2019.

dikec.about: Yusuf Dikeç is the Turkish sport shooter who won Olympic silver in 2024 with one hand in his pocket, plain glasses, and no special gear, next to competitors covered in equipment. The two-panel comparison captions the difference between overprepared and effortlessly competent.
dikec.origin: Photos from the Paris 2024 Olympics 10 m air pistol mixed team event went viral in July 2024.

congrats.about: The Office: Congratulations shows Michael Scott shaking hands with a dead-eyed, forced smile in the Dunder Mifflin office. The caption is a backhanded "congratulations" for an achievement that is not actually impressive.
congrats.origin: The still is from the US version of The Office and became a reaction image in the late 2010s.

goose-chase.about: Goose Chase is a two-panel drawing of a goose standing still and then chasing someone, with a label for the goose and a label for its victim. It captions anything that relentlessly pursues you, from deadlines to your own mistakes.
goose-chase.origin: The comic-style drawing spread on Reddit in 2019 alongside the wave of "geese are terrifying" memes.

aka: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?
millionaire.about: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? is the quiz-show template with a contestant staring at four answer boxes. The caption sets the question and fills in A, B, C and D, usually with one obviously wrong answer everyone picks anyway.
millionaire.origin: The format uses a still from the long-running game show and has been an exploitable on Reddit since the mid 2010s.

doakes.about: James Doakes Reaction Images are stills of Sergeant Doakes from Dexter, here glaring from his car during a stakeout. They caption suspicion, an unwelcome reveal, or someone who knows exactly what you did but can't prove it.
doakes.origin: Doakes, played by Erik King, appears in the first two seasons of Dexter (2006-2007); his stares and the "Surprise, motherf***er" line resurfaced as reaction formats in 2024.

aka: A Circle in the Triangle Factory
I Guess We Doin' Circles Now
triangle.about: A Circle in the Triangle Factory is a two-panel stick-figure comic: a worker in a triangle factory is baffled by a circle, then shrugs and decides "I guess we doin' circles now." It captions any rule, convention, or codebase that quietly changes as soon as one exception shows up.
triangle.origin: The comic spread on Twitter and Reddit in 2024 and was one of Know Your Meme's top memes of that year.

fix-door.about: You'll Get Your Rent When You Fix This Damn Door is a fill-in-the-blank meme from Spider-Man 2 (2004), in which Peter Parker's landlord Mr. Ditkovich demands rent and Peter fires back with the excuse. The two blanks are swapped for whatever someone is owed and whatever they are withholding it over.
fix-door.origin: The exchange happens early in Spider-Man 2, right after Peter comes home late from his failed pizza delivery. The fill-in version of the frame spread on Reddit and imgflip in 2022.

tobey-smirk.about: Peter Parker Smirk is a reaction image of Tobey Maguire's Peter Parker in the black symbiote suit, giving a sideways, smug little smile. It captions moments of quiet self-satisfaction, guilty pleasure, or knowing something the other person does not.
tobey-smirk.origin: The frame is from Spider-Man 3 (2007), during the stretch where the black suit starts to change Peter's personality. It joined the wider Bully Maguire meme wave around 2020.

my-back.about: My Back is a reaction image of Peter Parker wincing and holding his back after a jump goes wrong, captioned with the two-word complaint. It is used for anything that makes someone feel old, from standing up too fast to a mild physical effort.
my-back.origin: The scene is from Spider-Man 2 (2004), when Peter, losing his powers, tries to leap between rooftops and lands hard. The screenshot with its subtitle became a template in the early 2020s.

ripped-mask.about: Spider-Man Ripped Mask shows Tobey Maguire's Spider-Man with half of his mask torn away, bloodied and exhausted. It captions the state someone is in after a hard fight, a long shift, or a brutal week.
ripped-mask.origin: The image comes from the final battle of Spider-Man (2002) against the Green Goblin, where the mask is torn to reveal Peter's face.

visible-fear.about: Visible Fear is a reaction image of Peter Parker in his homemade wrestling mask, eyes wide with dread, captioned with the subtitle-style words 'Visible fear'. It is used for the moment right before something goes badly wrong.
visible-fear.origin: The frame is from the wrestling scene in Spider-Man (2002), when Peter sees Bonesaw McGraw for the first time. The subtitle caption comes from a widely shared screenshot.

aka: You Should Have Thought of That Earlier
thought-earlier.about: You Should Have Thought of That Earlier is a reaction image of Peter Parker coolly dismissing Eddie Brock, captioned with the line. It answers any belated excuse or plea for a second chance.
thought-earlier.origin: The line is from Spider-Man 3 (2007), when Eddie Brock begs Peter to spare his job after being exposed for faking a photo. It became a caption template alongside the other Bully Maguire scenes.

ad-said-3000.about: But the Ad Said 3000 is a reaction image of Peter Parker in his wrestling costume protesting that the flyer promised $3,000, captioned with the line. It is used whenever a payout, benefit, or promise turns out much smaller than advertised.
ad-said-3000.origin: The scene is from Spider-Man (2002), when the wrestling promoter pays Peter only $100 for beating Bonesaw in two minutes instead of three. The frame took off as a template in 2021.

aka: Please Sir, I Want Some More
oliver-twist.about: Please Sir, May I Have Some More is a reaction image of the orphan Oliver Twist holding up his empty bowl, used to caption a timid request for a little more of something: RAM, budget, sleep, or one more episode.
oliver-twist.origin: The scene comes from Charles Dickens' 1838 novel Oliver Twist, in which the starving boy asks the workhouse master for more gruel. The film adaptations, most often the 2005 Roman Polanski version, supply the image used as a template.

sun-tzu.about: Sun Tzu, The Art of War is a fake-quote template: a statue of the Chinese general on a black background, captioned with a modern or absurd piece of advice attributed to his 5th-century BC treatise. The joke is that any sentence sounds profound once it is signed '- Sun Tzu, The Art of War'.
sun-tzu.origin: Misattributed Sun Tzu quotes have circulated online since the early 2010s, and the terracotta-warrior-style image became the standard imgflip template for them.

so-far.about: Simpsons So Far is a two-panel template from The Simpsons: in the first panel Bart calmly says something, and in the second Homer strangles him. It is used for optimistic statements that are true only 'so far', with the punchline delivered as the strangling starts.
so-far.origin: The strangling gag is a running joke in The Simpsons since 1989. This two-panel format with the 'so far' punchline spread on imgflip in the late 2010s.

behind-tree.about: Guy Hiding Behind Tree is a reaction image of a man in a yellow jacket peeking out from behind a tree while rubbing his hands together, used for watching something unfold from a safe distance, or for sneaking up on an opportunity.
behind-tree.origin: The image is a still of comedian Anthony Adams from his 2019 'Deal or No Deal' sketch, the same source as the Anthony Adams Rubbing Hands meme. The tree variant spread on Twitter and imgflip in 2020.

hand-on-shoulder.about: Hand on Shoulder Guy is a two-character anime reaction image: one character places a comforting hand on another's shoulder while a third watches, used to caption consolation, reassurance, or a dubious pep talk.
hand-on-shoulder.origin: The frame is from a 1970s Japanese sports anime and was picked up as a labeling template on Reddit and imgflip in the early 2020s.

kermit-window.about: Kermit Looking Out Window is a reaction image of Kermit the Frog gazing out of a rain-streaked window, used to caption waiting, longing, or quiet sadness about something that is not coming.
kermit-window.origin: The still is from the 1979 film The Muppet Movie. It became a template for waiting jokes around 2014.

incoming-call.about: Incoming Call is a mock phone screen with a caller name at the top and Decline and Accept buttons at the bottom. The template is captioned with whoever or whatever is calling, from an ex to a 3 a.m. pager alert.
incoming-call.origin: Blank phone-screen templates have circulated on imgflip since the mid-2010s as a way to joke about unwanted or unexpected calls.

yes-honey.about: Yes Honey is a two-character drawing of a smiling woman in a red dress and a sad, sunken-eyed Wojak, in which the man agrees with whatever she says. It is used to caption resigned agreement with an unreasonable, or perfectly reasonable, request.
yes-honey.origin: The pairing combines the 'Trad Girl' character with the Wojak 'Feels Guy'. It spread on 4chan and Reddit around 2020.

brain-sleep.about: Brain Before Sleep is a four-panel comic in which a girl tries to sleep while a cartoon brain keeps her awake with an unwanted thought, and in the last panel she stares wide-eyed in the dark. The speech bubbles are captioned with the intrusive thought, usually something embarrassing from years ago.
brain-sleep.origin: The comic is a 2016 webcomic by artist Kamie that was cropped into a template and spread on Reddit and Twitter.

satisfied-seal.about: Satisfied Seal is a photograph of a seal with its eyes closed and a blissful smile, used to caption moments of pure contentment: a passing build, a paid invoice, a Friday afternoon with nothing due.
satisfied-seal.origin: The stock photo of a harbor seal spread on Reddit around 2012 and has been a happiness reaction image ever since.

wait-here.about: I'll Just Wait Here is a two-panel template in which a man sits at a computer, and in the second panel he has turned into a skeleton at the same desk. It captions anything that takes forever: a reply, a code review, a download, a promised feature.
wait-here.origin: The frames come from the 'skeleton waiting' gag used in comedies and adverts, and the two-panel version became an imgflip template in the mid-2010s.

confused-monkey.about: Confused Monkey is a short, blurry clip of a monkey grabbing its head with both hands and looking around in bewilderment, used as a reaction to something that makes no sense, or to realizing you have no idea what is going on.
confused-monkey.origin: The clip spread on TikTok and Reddit in 2024 and was added to imgflip as a video and GIF template.

aka: Are They in the Room With Us Right Now?
in-the-room.about: Are They in the Room With Us Right Now? is a two-panel-style reaction image of a man in a hospital gown sitting across from an interviewer in a bare room. It captions any grand claim about invisible enemies, users, or supporters by asking, deadpan, whether they are present.
in-the-room.origin: The still is from a 2020 YouTube interview with a self-described psychic. The 'in the room with us' caption spread on Twitter in 2023.

batman-signal.about: Bat Signal is a template of the Batman silhouette perched on a rooftop under a blank spotlight in the night sky. The signal is filled with whatever summons someone instantly: a keyword, a snack, a phrase.
batman-signal.origin: The Bat-Signal has been Gotham's way of calling Batman since 1942. The blank-signal template circulated on imgflip in the mid-2010s.

drooling-puzzle.about: Stupid Dumb Drooling Puzzle is a Wojak-style drawing of a drooling 'brainlet' trying to force a round block into a square hole. It captions doing something the obviously wrong way while being very confident about it.
drooling-puzzle.origin: The drawing is part of the Brainlet family of Wojak edits that spread on 4chan around 2017.

recording-fight.about: Guy Recording a Fight shows two women brawling on a lawn while a young man lies on the grass calmly filming them with his phone. It captions watching two sides argue without taking part, or enjoying drama from a safe distance.
recording-fight.origin: The photo is a still from a viral 2016 fight video and became a labeling template on Reddit soon after.

happy-dolphin.about: Happy Dolphin Rainbow is a saccharine stock-style picture of dolphins leaping under a rainbow with balloons and fish, used to caption an over-the-top happy reaction, often ironically.
happy-dolphin.origin: The picture is a kitsch wallpaper that meme makers adopted as a 'pure joy' template on imgflip in the 2020s.

cute-cat.about: Cute Cat Hehe / Not Hehe is a two-panel template with the same kitten looking pleased ('hehe') in the top panel and mildly annoyed ('not hehe') in the bottom one, with blank space beside each for what causes each mood.
cute-cat.origin: The kitten photos spread on Twitter in 2021 and imgflip turned them into a comparison template.

finally.about: FINALLY is a reaction image of a scientist in safety goggles holding up a test tube of green liquid, captioned 'Finally' and whatever hard-won thing has at last been achieved.
finally.origin: The stock photo became an imgflip template in 2020 for 'finally, a cure for X' style jokes.

laughing-suits.about: Laughing Men in Suits is a photo of a group of businessmen in tuxedos doubled over with laughter at a formal gathering. It captions a ridiculous suggestion that the people in charge would only laugh at.
laughing-suits.origin: The photograph shows Ronald Reagan and aides laughing in 1981. It has been a 'the rich laughing at you' reaction image since the early 2010s.

yelling-beaver.about: Yelling Beaver, better known as the Screaming Marmot, is a short clip of a marmot standing on its hind legs and letting out a long scream. It is used as a reaction to sudden rage or exasperation.
yelling-beaver.origin: The clip comes from a 2013 video of a marmot in the Canadian Rockies and went viral on YouTube and Vine.

shrek-running.about: Shrek Running is a blurry clip of Shrek sprinting at full speed with a panicked look. It captions running from responsibility, from a meeting, or toward something desirable.
shrek-running.origin: The scene is from Shrek (2001) and became a GIF reaction on Tumblr and imgflip in the late 2010s.

surprised-koala.about: Surprised Koala is a photo of a koala with a eucalyptus leaf in its mouth, staring wide-eyed at the camera. It captions being caught off guard, or pretending to be shocked by something obvious.
surprised-koala.origin: The photo spread on Reddit around 2013 and has been a mild-surprise reaction image ever since.

shipping-label.about: Penguin Pointing at Shipping Label shows Skipper from Penguins of Madagascar pointing at a blank address label on a crate. The label is filled with wherever or whatever something is being sent.
shipping-label.origin: The frame is from the Penguins of Madagascar series and became an imgflip template in 2020.

dumbest-man.about: I'm the Dumbest Man Alive is a four-panel comic in which a stick figure proudly declares himself the dumbest man alive, only for another to prove him wrong with something even dumber in the last panel. The empty speech bubble is captioned with the dumber statement.
dumbest-man.origin: The comic is by webcomic artist Srgrafo and was cropped into a template on Reddit in 2019.

goodfellas.about: Goodfellas Laughing shows Ray Liotta and Joe Pesci's characters cracking up at a nightclub table. It captions a suggestion so absurd that everyone in the room bursts out laughing.
goodfellas.origin: The still is from the 1990 film Goodfellas, from the 'funny how?' scene, and has been a laughter reaction image since the 2010s.

aka: Believe It or Not, Straight to Jail
straight-to-jail.about: Straight to Jail is a reaction image of Fred Armisen's character from Parks and Recreation, a Venezuelan official who lists petty offenses that all lead 'straight to jail, right away'. It captions any minor offense treated as a crime.
straight-to-jail.origin: The scene is from the 2009 Parks and Recreation episode 'Sister City' and became a caption template around 2019.

big-book-small-book.about: Big Book, Small Book is a comparison template showing a thick, heavy book beside a slim one. The two are labeled to contrast what takes a lot of explanation with what takes very little.
big-book-small-book.origin: The stock photo comparison spread on Reddit in 2020 as a way to mock lopsided documentation, rules, or excuses.

pink-guy-bane.about: Pink Guy vs. Bane is a mashup of Bane's 'for you' stance from The Dark Knight Rises with Filthy Frank's Pink Guy in place of Batman. It captions a mismatched confrontation, or a threat that is much smaller than it thinks it is.
pink-guy-bane.origin: The image combines the 2012 Bane scene with Pink Guy, a character from Filthy Frank's YouTube videos, and spread on 4chan and Reddit around 2015.

be-honest.about: Be Honest is a three-panel template from the Beckham documentary in which Victoria Beckham claims to be working class, David leans in and says 'be honest', and she concedes the truth. It captions any inflated self-description followed by a reality check.
be-honest.origin: The exchange is from the 2023 Netflix documentary Beckham and went viral on TikTok and Twitter within days.

confused-travolta.about: Confused John Travolta is a short clip of Vincent Vega looking around a room in bewilderment. It is used to caption looking for something that is not there: documentation, a coworker, the point of a meeting.
confused-travolta.origin: The clip is from the 1994 film Pulp Fiction and became a widely edited GIF around 2015, often with Travolta pasted into other scenes.

hulk-secret.about: That's My Secret, Cap is a reaction image of Bruce Banner mid-transformation, captioned with his line 'That's my secret, Cap. I'm always angry.' It captions a hidden constant state: always tired, always debugging, always hungry.
hulk-secret.origin: The line is from the 2012 film The Avengers, delivered just before the Battle of New York.

squidward-spare.about: Squidward Spare is a reaction image of a ragged Squidward holding out a cup and asking for spare change. It captions begging for anything in short supply: a code review, a day off, one more retry.
squidward-spare.origin: The frame is from the SpongeBob SquarePants episode 'Can You Spare a Dime?' (2002), in which Squidward quits his job and ends up destitute. It became an imgflip template around 2020.

went-to-college.about: Plankton 'I Went to College' is a reaction image of Plankton shouting his catchphrase, used to caption someone defending questionable competence with their credentials.
went-to-college.origin: The line comes from the SpongeBob SquarePants episode 'Plankton!' (1999), when Plankton insists he is smart enough to run Krabs' restaurant. It became a widely quoted meme in the 2010s.

empire-state-flag.about: Empire State Building Climbers Flag is an exploitable image of rooftoppers Angela Nikolau and Ivan Kuznetsov at the top of the Empire State Building's spire beside a huge black banner. The banner's message is swapped out for any slogan, PSA or brand announcement, turning the stunt into a way to broadcast an opinion to all of New York.
empire-state-flag.origin: On July 1st, 2026, the pair climbed the Empire State Building, unfurled a black flag reading "When the power of love beats the love of power the world knows peace" and got engaged at the top. Photos of the climb went viral within days, and brands and posters quickly started editing their own text onto the flag.

potential-megumi.about: Did You Say Potential? is a reaction image of Megumi Fushiguro from Jujutsu Kaisen grinning manically while pulling at his face. It is used to react to any mention of "potential" or to mock something that is always about to be great but never actually delivers.
potential-megumi.origin: The format grows out of the Meet Potential Man joke, which since 2023 has teased Megumi for being hyped by fans as a character with huge potential rather than actual power. In 2026, a still from Jujutsu Kaisen's third season became the go-to reply in fan edits built around the line "Did you say potential?"

aka: Right Where I'm Supposed to Be
Backrooms I Like It in Here
like-it-in-here.about: I Like It in Here is a reaction image of Chiwetel Ejiofor, teary-eyed and smiling, with the subtitle "I like it in here. I feel like I'm right where I'm supposed to be." It captions places, habits or situations someone has sunk into and has no intention of leaving, usually ones that are not great for them.
like-it-in-here.origin: The still comes from Backrooms (2026), A24's feature adaptation of Kane Parsons's web series, in which Ejiofor plays a furniture store owner drawn into the endless yellow rooms. The line spread as a meme on TikTok and YouTube Shorts around the film's release.
